newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia's Fischer says won't be pushed on populist issues.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia's Fischer says won't be pushed on populist issues.

text.p: Australian National Party leader and Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said on Friday his party would not be pushed into stoking populist arguments that were divisive to Australia's trade relations and ties with Asia.

"We've had guns, we've had the greater Asia debate but Australia's bread ticket, quite apart from the moral reasons, is going to come over the next 50 years from a better economic engagement with Asia," Fischer told reporters at the National Party's federal conference in Canberra.
The Liberal-National government instituted tough new gun laws after the Port Arthur massacre.
Fischer said he would not buy into the populist race debate sparked by the comments of independent politician Pauline Hanson which have led to an emotional debate on race and immigration.
"I reject it in terms of stoking up an Asian debate that is divisive, that is dumb, that is wrong," Fischer said.
"And those who thought I would be an easy shove around on key issues are learning, some a bit slowly, that I'm not for turning with regard to these key issues."
Fischer said it would have been easy to be popular on key issues such as gun control and immigration and the greater Asia debate, but it would have been morally wrong.

The tide on race was turning both within Australia and overseas as it had not been an issue on his visit in the past week to Singapore, Bangkok or India at the official level or on the margins, he said.
"There was barely a reference to it and they understood our message as part of a new horizons promotion that Australia is going to boost its trade investment tourism activity in India."
In Australia there had been a bit of a sea change starting and people would go on legitimately debating the size of the immigration intake, he said.
"But let's drop the racist and other twists and turns along the way," he said.

He said the Australian parliament's bipartisan motion on race, which condemned racism and reaffirmed its position on equal rights, cultural diversity and a non-discriminatory immigration policy, was received extremely well overseas.

"I made it very clear I was not going up there to apologise because governmental policy has never deviated, but I utilised the bipartisan motion simply to affirm where the Australian parliament, as opposed and separate from the Australian government, position is on the issue," he said.
"The best way we will get on in Asia is not to grovel to Asia, but to forthrightly state our case and this I did. I did not go up there to apologise to Asia," Fischer said.
